title: Quran Waqf and Stop Signs
intro: Waqf means stopping or pausing during Quran recitation. Mushaf symbols guide the reciter toward stops and continuations that preserve meaning. Exact symbols and conventions differ between mushaf traditions.
importantNote: These are reading aids, not a substitute for learning Tajweed and Waqf/Ibtida from a qualified teacher. Do not describe every symbol as an absolute legal obligation; schools and mushaf traditions use different terminology and degrees of recommendation.

rules.name: Waqf Lazim
rules.simpleExplanation: Continuing can connect the wording in a way that harms or changes the intended meaning in the common Madinah convention.
rules.breath: Take a breath after stopping if needed.

rules.name: Waqf Mutlaq
rules.simpleExplanation: The meaning is considered complete here. Common in some Indo-Pak/Sajawandi mushafs.

rules.name: Ruku sign
rules.simpleExplanation: In Indo-Pak mushafs, ع commonly marks the end of a ruku or thematic section. It is not one of the core Madinah mushaf waqf symbols and is not an absolute stop command.

rules.name: Waqf Jaiz
rules.simpleExplanation: Both stopping and continuing are acceptable.

rules.name: Wasl Awla
rules.simpleExplanation: Stopping is allowed, but continuing is considered better.

rules.name: Waqf Awla
rules.simpleExplanation: Both options are permitted, but stopping is considered better.

rules.name: La
rules.simpleExplanation: Avoid stopping because the phrase is incomplete or meaning can be distorted by stopping.

rules.name: Qif
rules.simpleExplanation: A stop is indicated in mushafs that use the Qif convention.

rules.name: Qeela Alayhil-Waqf
rules.simpleExplanation: Some reciters regard it as a possible stopping point, but continuing is generally stronger in this convention.

rules.name: Waqf Mujawwaz
rules.simpleExplanation: Stopping is permitted, but continuing is preferable.

rules.name: Waqf Murakhkhas
rules.action: Continue normally; stop if breath requires it.
rules.simpleExplanation: A long sentence may permit a breath stop here when necessary.

rules.name: Saktah
rules.action: Pause briefly, without taking a new breath, then continue.
rules.simpleExplanation: Saktah is not a full waqf; the breath is maintained.

rules.name: Waqf Mu'anaqah
rules.action: Stop at one of the two paired locations, not both.
rules.simpleExplanation: Choose one stopping location. Do not stop at both paired marks.

commonBeginnerRules.rule: Avoid stopping at a marked لا location.
commonBeginnerRules.reason: The phrase may be incomplete and the meaning can be distorted.

commonBeginnerRules.rule: When stopping on a word, the final short vowel is generally dropped.
commonBeginnerRules.reason: Waqf changes the ending pronunciation according to Tajweed rules.

commonBeginnerRules.rule: Do not restart from an isolated word or phrase if it produces an incomplete or misleading meaning.
commonBeginnerRules.reason: Waqf and Ibtida covers both where to stop and where to restart.

commonBeginnerRules.rule: A verse-end is generally a recognized stopping place.
commonBeginnerRules.reason: The end of an ayah is a natural structural boundary, though the appropriate restart still matters.

commonBeginnerRules.rule: If breath runs out at a poor stopping point, return to an appropriate earlier point before continuing.
commonBeginnerRules.reason: Meaning-aware recitation is more important than forcing a breathless continuation.

mushafVariation: The Madinah Mushaf commonly uses م, لا, ج, صلى, قلى, paired dots and س. Indo-Pak/Sajawandi editions may additionally use signs such as ط, ز, ص, ق, قف and ع.
